title: A Real Day as a Food Stylist (it's not glamorous)
creator: Priya Venkataraman
description:
What a commercial food styling day actually looks like: tweezers, fake ice, and twelve versions of the same salad.

I'm a freelance food stylist based in Melbourne. Questions about getting into the industry? Leave them in the comments and I'll answer a few in the next video.

Filmed on my phone between takes, sorry about the audio.

sentences.t: Good morning, it is six forty and I'm already in the studio, which is a warehouse in Collingwood that smells like burnt toast.
People always ask me what a food stylist actually does all day, so today I'm just going to show you.
Spoiler, it's mostly waiting and tweezers.
Let me set up the job first.
So today's client is Ceralune, which is an olive oil brand, and they hired our studio to shoot the photos for their new recipe cards.
The ones that come tucked in the box when you buy the bottle, you know the little cards.
There are eight recipes, and I'm responsible for making every single dish look perfect on set, while the photographer, Dan, shoots them.
Their brand manager Lucia is here too, and she has very strong opinions about how shiny the oil should look, which, fair, it's literally their product.
Honestly this is one of my favourite clients, because they actually let us cook real food instead of faking everything.
Okay so first up is a panzanella salad.
This is the hero bowl.
And this here is the stand-in bowl, which is the one we use while Dan sorts out the lighting.
Nobody eats the stand-in.
The stand-in has been under hot lights for an hour and it is sad.
For the hero, I'm picking out every single cube of bread one by one.
I want the ones with the crispiest edges facing the camera.
This is the tweezers part.
I'm not joking, I own about fifteen pairs of tweezers.
Now the oil.
So you'd think you just pour oil on a salad.
No.
If you pour it, it soaks into the bread and goes dark and patchy within like two minutes.
So what I do is I brush it on right before the shot, with a little paint brush, only on the tomatoes and the top layer.
That gives you that glossy look without everything going soggy.
Lucia is nodding, so I think we're good.
It's now eleven o'clock, and we have shot two out of eight.
That's normal, by the way.
The first one always takes forever, because that's when we lock in the lighting and the angle and the props.
After that it speeds up.
Dan wants to try a top-down for the soup, so I'm going to swap the spoon for a smaller one, because a big spoon in a top-down looks like a shovel.
These are the things nobody tells you in culinary school.
Lunch break.
And no, we don't eat the props.
Okay, sometimes we eat the props.
The roast potatoes from recipe four are honestly incredible and I have eaten three of them.
Right, afternoon.
This is the hard one, which is a lemon tart.
The problem with a tart is the slice.
You need one perfectly clean slice coming out, with a sharp edge, no crumbs, no cracks.
So I've made three tarts.
I'm cutting with a knife that I'm heating under hot water and wiping between every cut.
Ooh, okay, that one's good.
Don't touch it, nobody breathe.
And that's a wrap, it's six in the evening, and we got all eight.
My feet are destroyed.
If you want to get into food styling, my honest advice is, assist someone first.
You learn more in one week on set than in a year of watching videos, including this one.
I'll be back next week with a full tour of my styling kit, including all fifteen tweezers.
Bye!
